title: Phone order confirmation texts for restaurants
seoTitle: Phone order confirmation texts for restaurants
description: Send a clear phone order confirmation text after pickup or delivery calls. Use examples and templates that confirm the order, time, and next steps.
question: What should a phone order confirmation text restaurant owners send after a call?
answer: A good phone order confirmation text should repeat the order, pickup or delivery time, total if needed, and a clear way to reply if something is wrong. Keep it short, plain, and tied to the exact phone order so the guest can spot mistakes fast. For many restaurants, the best version is a text that confirms the items, name, and ready time right after the call.
summary: You’ll be able to write clear order confirmation texts for phone orders and build a simple process around them.
intro:
A phone order confirmation text restaurant owners send should repeat the order in plain language, include the ready time, and make it easy for the guest to spot a mistake. It should be short enough to read quickly on a busy night.

If your shop takes pickup or delivery orders by phone, a confirmation text is one of the simplest ways to cut confusion. ROAL can handle the call, confirm the order back, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, but you still want a clear text style for your own process and staff notes.

sections.h2: What should a phone order confirmation text include?
sections.body:
A good confirmation text does not need to be fancy. It needs to be clear, short, and specific to the order that was just taken.

Use this simple structure:

1. Customer name
2. Order type: pickup or delivery
3. Key items and modifiers
4. Ready time
5. A short correction line, if the guest needs to reply

Example text:

"Hi Maria, your pickup order from Tony’s Pizza is confirmed: 1 large cheese pizza, 1 order of garlic knots, no onions. Ready at 6:40 PM. Reply if anything looks wrong."

If you want to make it even easier for staff, keep a standard format every time. That helps when the same person calls twice in a week. ROAL already confirms the order back on the call, and the kitchen gets a clean ticket, so your text can stay simple and consistent.

Checklist before you send:
- Did you repeat the main items?
- Did you include pickup or delivery?
- Did you include the ready time?
- Did you keep it short enough to read fast?
- Did you avoid extra wording that could hide a mistake?

sections.h2: How do you write one without making it too long?
sections.body:
The best confirmation texts are short because people read them while they are driving, working, or packing bags for pickup. Long texts get skipped.

A good rule is to use one sentence for the order and one sentence for the timing. If the order is large, you can still keep it readable by grouping items.

Here are three workable formats:

| Situation | Example text |
|---|---|
| Small pickup order | "Thanks, Joe. Your pickup order is confirmed: 2 plain slices and 1 soda. Ready at 5:15 PM." |
| Delivery order | "Hi Priya, your delivery order is confirmed: chicken tikka, naan, and mango lassi. Estimated delivery at 7:10 PM." |
| Special request | "Hi Sam, your pickup order is confirmed: turkey hero, no mayo, extra pickles. Ready at 12:30 PM. We noted the allergy request for staff review." |

If you need a deeper confirmation, keep it inside the call, not in the text. That is where the order is repeated back, questions are answered, and the ready time is spoken clearly. The text is the receipt-like summary.

For owners who want to compare systems, [phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps) and [AI phone host vs voicemail](/compare/voicemail) are useful reads.

sections.h2: How do you keep confirmation texts from causing mistakes?
sections.body:
A text can help fix confusion, but it can also create it if the wording is sloppy. The goal is to make the text match the kitchen ticket and the caller’s understanding.

Use this process:

1. Take the order.
2. Repeat the order back on the call.
3. Confirm the name and phone number.
4. Set the ready time.
5. Send the text summary only after the order is clear.

A practical example:
- Caller says: "One pepperoni pizza, well done, and a Greek salad, no onions."
- Phone host repeats: "One large pepperoni pizza, well done, and one Greek salad, no onions. Ready in 25 minutes."
- Text sent: "Hi Carlos, your pickup order is confirmed: 1 large pepperoni pizza, well done, 1 Greek salad, no onions. Ready at 6:05 PM."

That format keeps the same details in three places: spoken confirmation, text, and kitchen ticket. If the caller notices a problem, staff can compare all three fast.

Short checklist for staff:
- Does the text match the spoken confirmation?
- Did the kitchen receive the same items and modifiers?
- Did you use the same ready time in both places?
- Did you avoid abbreviations the guest may not understand?

sections.h2: What should you text for pickup orders versus delivery orders?
sections.body:
Pickup and delivery need slightly different wording because the guest is doing something different next.

For pickup, tell them when the order should be ready and where to come in. For delivery, tell them the estimated drop-off time and avoid promising more than your team can handle.

Example pickup text:
"Hi Denise, your pickup order from Bella Deli is confirmed: 2 Italian subs, 1 bag of chips, and 1 bottled water. Ready at 1:20 PM."

Example delivery text:
"Hi Denise, your delivery order from Bella Deli is confirmed: 2 Italian subs, 1 bag of chips, and 1 bottled water. Estimated delivery at 1:45 PM."

If your restaurant already has a standard pickup window, use that language. If you use a ready time, keep the text aligned with the time the caller heard. That matters in busy shops, especially when the phone rings again before the first order is finished.

A simple format table can help your staff stay consistent:

| Order type | What to include | What to avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Pickup | items, modifiers, ready time, pickup note | long explanations, unnecessary details |
| Delivery | items, modifiers, estimated drop-off time | promises your team cannot meet |
| Curbside | items, car note, ready time | vague instructions like "sometime soon" |

ROAL can take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu and confirm the order back on the call, which helps keep the text and the ticket aligned.

sections.h2: How do you handle sold-out items, notes, and allergies?
sections.body:
This is where clear wording matters most. If something is sold out, it should not be offered in the first place. If a caller asks for a tricky change, the phone host should hand it to staff with a summary.

For the text, keep special notes visible but not overly wordy.

Examples:
- "No onions"
- "Sauce on the side"
- "Allergy note sent to staff"

Example confirmation text:
"Hi Ana, your pickup order is confirmed: 1 grilled chicken wrap, no tomatoes, 1 fries, no salt. Ready at 4:50 PM. Allergy note sent to staff."

That line is clear without trying to solve the allergy in the text itself. The text is not the place to debate ingredients. It is the place to show the order was captured correctly.

If a caller asks for a catering change, a manager request, or a serious allergy question, staff should handle it directly. ROAL is built to pass those calls to the team with a summary, which is the safer move for anything complicated.

Quick staff checklist:
- Did the note get into the kitchen ticket?
- Did the text show the note in plain language?
- Was the caller told the right ready time?
- Did any special issue get sent to staff instead of guessed at?

sections.h2: Should you send the text right away or after the order is checked?
sections.body:
For most restaurants, send the confirmation text right after the order is confirmed and the ticket is ready to go. That gives the guest a record while the call is still fresh.

But if your team needs a quick second look on certain orders, it is fine to use a two-step process:

1. Take the order.
2. Check any tricky item or note.
3. Send the text once the order is approved.

This matters more on busy nights. Say your average phone order is $28. If you get 20 phone orders in a night, that is $560 in sales to protect. Plug in your own average order and your own call volume. The point is simple: a clear text helps reduce back-and-forth and keeps the order moving.

Some owners also like a very short follow-up line after a long order, such as:
"Thanks, your order is in. We’ll see you at 7:10 PM."

That works when the full details have already been captured and confirmed. If you want a broader setup, [How it works](/how-it-works) explains how ROAL reads your menu, answers the phone, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen without a setup headache.

sections.h2: What is the easiest way to set this up for your restaurant?
sections.body:
The easiest setup is one that matches how your restaurant already answers the phone.

Here is a simple rollout plan:

1. Write one default text template for pickup.
2. Write one default text template for delivery.
3. Add one line for special notes.
4. Train staff to keep the wording short.
5. Test a few example orders before busy hours.

You do not need a complicated system. You need a repeatable one. Final checklist before launch:
- Does the text match the way your staff talks?
- Does it include the ready time?
- Does it stay short?
- Does it fit pickup and delivery separately?
- Does it point special issues to staff instead of guessing?

takeaways: Keep confirmation texts short, specific, and tied to the exact order.
Always include the items, order type, and ready time.
Use the text as a summary, not a place to solve complicated issues.
Match the text to the spoken confirmation and kitchen ticket.
Use one standard format so staff can send it fast on busy shifts.

faq.q: What should a restaurant order confirmation text say?
faq.a: It should say the customer’s name, the items, the order type, and the ready time. Keep it short and easy to read. If there is a special note like no onions or an allergy mention, include it in plain language so the guest can spot it fast.

faq.q: Should I send a confirmation text before or after the phone order is taken?
faq.a: Send it after the order is confirmed and the details are clear. That way the text matches what the guest heard and what the kitchen will make. If there is a tricky item or special note, check it first, then send the text.

faq.q: Can I use the same confirmation text for pickup and delivery?
faq.a: You can use the same basic structure, but change the timing line. Pickup should say when the order is ready and where to come in. Delivery should say the estimated drop-off time. That small change helps the guest know what happens next.
